title: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County
focus: the art of the deadpan tall tale

teacherSummary.text: The genteel narrator asks old Simon Wheeler about a Reverend Leonidas W. Smiley and instead hears, in dead earnest, the story of Jim Smiley, who would bet on anything. Smiley trains a frog, Dan'l Webster, to jump. A stranger fills the frog with quail shot while Smiley fetches a second frog, and wins the bet. When Wheeler starts on a one-eyed cow, the narrator escapes.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County,” how does Twain show the art of the deadpan tall tale? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the diction / vocabulary you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County, how does Twain develop the idea of the art of the deadpan tall tale? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the diction / vocabulary in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County develops the idea of the art of the deadpan tall tale. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of diction / vocabulary and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County (where it begins, turns and ends) and its diction / vocabulary shape the reader's understanding of the art of the deadpan tall tale. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County suggests about the art of the deadpan tall tale. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's diction / vocabulary and point of view), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mark Twain uses diction / vocabulary in The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County to complicate the reader's understanding of the art of the deadpan tall tale. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the art of the deadpan tall tale responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the art of the deadpan tall tale follows or bends those conventions, using the diction / vocabulary as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County and its treatment of the art of the deadpan tall tale. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's diction / vocabulary and point of view, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County as evidence for a larger claim about the art of the deadpan tall tale in The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the art of the deadpan tall tale. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County.

satQuestions.passage: In compliance with the request of a friend of mine, who wrote me from the East, I called on good-natured, garrulous old Simon Wheeler, and inquired after my friend's friend, Leonidas W. Smiley, as requested to do, and I hereunto append the result. I have a lurking suspicion that Leonidas W. Smiley is a myth; that my friend never knew such a personage; and that he only conjectured that, if I asked old Wheeler about him, it would remind him of his infamous Jim Smiley, and he would go to work and bore me nearly to death with some infernal reminiscence of him as long and tedious as it should be useless to me. If that was the design, it certainly succeeded.

A boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What makes someone a good storyteller? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes animal cruelty played for comedy (frog loaded with shot).

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are straddle, garrulous, uncover, sociable, cherished. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “And when it come to fair and square jumping on a dead level, he could get over more ground at one straddle than any animal of his breed you ever see.” In this sentence it means: to sit or stand with one leg on each side. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County would have known. Published in the New York Saturday Press in 1865; it made Twain nationally famous. Why does this story matter? A landmark of American vernacular humor and the frame narrative; in Gale's Short Stories for Students vol. 1. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for diction / vocabulary.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “In compliance with the request of a friend of mine, who wrote me from the East, I called on good-natured, garrulous old Simon Wheeler, and inquired after my friend's friend, Leonidas W.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the art of the deadpan tall tale? I circle “garrulous”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find diction / vocabulary, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for diction / vocabulary.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of diction / vocabulary. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to tall tales and frontier humor? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
